title: Sowing Generously: God Loves a Cheerful Giver
summary: Paul explains that he is sending the brothers ahead so that the gift the Corinthians promised will be ready when he arrives with the Macedonians, and will be given generously, not grudgingly. Using the picture of sowing and reaping, he teaches that God loves a cheerful giver and is able to supply all they need so that they can abound in every good work. Their gift will meet the needs of the saints in Jerusalem and overflow in thanksgiving to God, and it all rests on God's indescribable gift.
story: Chapter 9 continues the appeal about the collection for the believers in Jerusalem begun in chapter 8. Paul has boasted to the Macedonians about the Corinthians' readiness, and now he wants to make sure that boast proves true. The chapter moves from practical arrangements to the theology behind giving, and it ends in worship. After it, the tone of the letter changes sharply: chapters 10-13 confront the false apostles who have been undermining Paul in Corinth.
historical:
Paul was writing from Macedonia, probably around AD 55 or 56, planning to travel south to Corinth with some Macedonian believers before taking the collection to Jerusalem. Achaia (verse 2) was the Roman province of southern Greece, whose capital was Corinth, and it likely included other congregations such as the one at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port (Romans 16:1). Romans 15:26, written from Corinth a few months later, reports that "Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem". So the appeal of these chapters appears to have succeeded.

The risk Paul names in verses 3-5 was real. If the Macedonians, who had given out of poverty, arrived in wealthier Corinth and found nothing ready, both Paul and the Corinthians would be publicly shamed, and the collection's purpose of uniting the churches would suffer.
cultural:
The Corinthians lived in an agricultural economy even in a commercial city, and the imagery of sowing and harvest was part of everyone's world. A farmer who hoarded his seed for fear of losing it would reap little; one who sowed freely would reap a larger harvest. Paul's proverb in verse 6 draws on this common wisdom, which also appears in Proverbs 11:24-25 and 22:8. The phrase "God loves a cheerful giver" in verse 7 closely echoes a line that the Greek translation of Proverbs adds at 22:8, about God blessing a cheerful and generous man.

In Greek and Roman patronage, a benefactor's gift obligated the recipients to honor him. Paul reverses the direction of that expectation. The Jerusalem saints will not become the Corinthians' clients; instead, their response will be thanksgiving to God and prayer for the givers (verses 12-14). The one who ultimately receives honor is God, the source of every gift. The word leitourgia in verse 12, used in the Greek world for a public service funded by a wealthy citizen and in the Greek Old Testament for priestly service in worship, suggests that giving is both a public service and an act of worship.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1-5 handle arrangements with tact, using the language of boasting and readiness, and ending with a contrast between a generous gift (eulogia, literally a blessing) and one given grudgingly. Verses 6-11 build a theology of giving from an agricultural image, with two Old Testament echoes: Psalm 112:9, quoted in verse 9 ("He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor"), and Isaiah 55:10, echoed in verse 10's God "who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food". The word "all" (pas) is piled up in verse 8: all grace, all things, all times, all that you need, every good work. Verses 12-15 widen the view from the Corinthians to the saints in Jerusalem and finally to God, ending in a single exclamation of thanks.

outline.t: Be ready: the brothers are sent ahead
Sow generously; God loves a cheerful giver
God supplies all you need for every good work
Thanksgiving to God for his indescribable gift

doctrines.note: "God is able to make all grace abound to you" (verse 8). God supplies both seed and bread, so that givers have what they need and more to share. Giving rests on trust that God provides, not on calculation of loss.

The recipients of the gift will pray for the givers and long for them (verse 14). Material help creates spiritual bonds; the collection becomes a channel of prayer and affection between Jewish and Gentile believers who had never met.

The chapter ends by naming the gift behind all others: "Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!" Most interpreters take this as Christ himself, or God's saving grace in him. Human generosity is always a response to that gift.

words.note: Hilaros, cheerful, glad (the source of the English word hilarious, though the Greek has no sense of comedy). It appears only here in the New Testament. A cheerful giver gives freely from the heart, not under pressure or with regret.

Eulogia, literally a good word, a blessing; it can also mean a bountiful gift. Paul calls the collection a eulogia (verse 5), and uses the same word in verse 6, where sowing "generously" is literally sowing with blessings. A gift given freely is itself a blessing.

Leitourgia, service, ministry (the source of the English word liturgy). In civic Greek it was a public service funded by a wealthy citizen; in the Greek Old Testament it described the service of priests and Levites. Its use here gives the collection the character of worship.

Anekdiegetos, indescribable, beyond telling in full. It appears only here in the New Testament. After two chapters of careful words about giving, Paul ends by admitting that God's own gift cannot be put into words.

christ: The chapter ends with thanks for God's "indescribable gift", which, after 8:9's description of Christ becoming poor to make others rich, most readers understand as Christ himself and the grace God gives in him. The generosity Paul asks for is patterned on God's generosity in Christ. The Corinthians' giving will also be an "obedient confession of the gospel of Christ" (verse 13): generosity shows that they have truly received the gospel. The whole economy of the chapter, God giving, people receiving and passing on, thanksgiving returning to God, has Christ as its center and source.

hard.q: Does "whoever sows generously will also reap generously" promise that giving money will make you rich?
hard.a:
Prosperity teaching often uses this chapter to claim that gifts to God, or to a particular ministry, guarantee a larger financial return. The text does not support that reading. Paul says God will provide "all that you need" so that you "will abound in every good work" (verse 8); the harvest is described as "the harvest of your righteousness" (verse 10); and the enrichment of verse 11 is "to be generous on every occasion", so that thanksgiving goes to God. The return on generosity is the capacity for more generosity, not personal wealth.

Paul's own life makes the point. He was often hungry and poor (6:10; 11:27), and the Macedonians he praises as models gave out of "deep poverty" (8:2). The chapter does teach that God is not stingy and that he meets the needs of those who give, and many Christians testify to God's provision. But reading it as a formula for material gain turns grace into a transaction, the opposite of Paul's argument.

questions: Paul wants the gift to be ready and given generously, not grudgingly or under compulsion. What makes giving feel like a burden, and what makes it cheerful?
Verse 8 promises that God will supply what is needed for every good work. How does trust in God's provision change the way you hold your money?
The Corinthians' gift would lead strangers in Jerusalem to pray for them. How does giving across distance and difference build unity in the church?
